conclusion.label: leans_reject

report:
## Conclusion

The evidence suggests CLA supplements produce, at best, a **small and likely clinically insignificant** reduction in body fat/abdominal fat—not a robust or reliable effect.

Multiple meta-analyses of randomized controlled trials converge on this conclusion. A 2023 systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis found CLA supplementation caused only "a small but significant improvement in anthropometric and body composition markers," but concluded that "data from high-quality studies failed to show CLA's body fat-lowering properties," and noted the effects "may not reach clinical importance" (https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/british-journal-of-nutrition/article/effects-of-conjugated-linoleic-acid-supplementation-on-anthropometrics-and-body-composition-indices-in-adults-a-systematic-review-and-doseresponse-metaanalysis/A3F12F07BB3118D4F757D901C6E1E366). Similarly, an earlier meta-analysis in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition noted that while CLA reduces fat mass in animal studies, "results in humans have been inconsistent" (https://ajcn.nutrition.org/article/S0002-9165(23)28055-7/fulltext).

Some individual trials do report abdominal-specific effects: a small trial in obese men with metabolic syndrome found CLA "may decrease abdominal fat" over 4 weeks, though the authors cautioned this needs confirmation in larger trials due to limited sample size (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11477497/). A 12-week trial in overweight/obese women similarly reported reductions in visceral, android, and gynoid fat (https://www.mdpi.com/2072-6643/12/6/1811).

However, these positive findings come from smaller, shorter trials, while pooled analyses of higher-quality evidence do not confirm meaningful fat loss. Overall, the claim is only weakly and inconsistently supported—CLA is not a reliably effective intervention for reducing abdominal fat in humans.
